claim: Rlim is an X-linked gene that encodes a RING H2 type E3 ligase.
source: The X-linked gene Rlim (also known as Rnf12) encodes a RING H2 type E3 ligase (Metzger et al., 2014; Joazeiro and Weissman, 2000; Bach et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Metzger et al., 2014; Joazeiro and Weissman, 2000; Bach et al., 1999).

claim: Female mice carrying a systemic Rlim knockout die around implantation.
source: while females carrying a systemic Rlim knockout (KO) die around implantation, male Rlim KO mice appear healthy and are fertile.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract as a direct observation from the study.

claim: Male Rlim KO mice appear healthy and are fertile.
source: while females carrying a systemic Rlim knockout (KO) die around implantation, male Rlim KO mice appear healthy and are fertile.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract as a direct observation from the study.

claim: Rlim is highly expressed in post-meiotic round spermatids.
source: Here, we report an important role for Rlim in testis where it is highly expressed in post-meiotic round spermatids as well as in Sertoli cells.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Rlim is highly expressed in Sertoli cells.
source: Here, we report an important role for Rlim in testis where it is highly expressed in post-meiotic round spermatids as well as in Sertoli cells.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Systemic deletion of Rlim results in lower numbers of mature sperm.
source: Systemic deletion of the Rlim gene results in lower numbers of mature sperm that contains excess cytoplasm, leading to decreased sperm motility and in vitro fertilization rates.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 3C showing significantly decreased sperm numbers.

claim: Systemic deletion of Rlim results in sperm that contains excess cytoplasm.
source: Systemic deletion of the Rlim gene results in lower numbers of mature sperm that contains excess cytoplasm, leading to decreased sperm motility and in vitro fertilization rates.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by electron microscopy data in Figures 5 and 6 showing increased cytoplasmic droplet size.

claim: Systemic deletion of Rlim leads to decreased sperm motility.
source: Systemic deletion of the Rlim gene results in lower numbers of mature sperm that contains excess cytoplasm, leading to decreased sperm motility and in vitro fertilization rates.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by CASA analysis data in Figure 4C-E.

claim: Systemic deletion of Rlim leads to decreased in vitro fertilization rates.
source: Systemic deletion of the Rlim gene results in lower numbers of mature sperm that contains excess cytoplasm, leading to decreased sperm motility and in vitro fertilization rates.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by IVF data in Figure 4F-G.

claim: Targeting conditional Rlim cKO to the spermatogenic cell lineage largely recapitulates the phenotype of systemic Rlim deletion.
source: Targeting the conditional Rlim cKO specifically to the spermatogenic cell lineage largely recapitulates this phenotype.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 7 comparing Ngn3-Cre and Sf1-Cre mediated deletions.

claim: Rlim has functions in male reproduction specifically in round spermatids during spermiogenesis.
source: These results reveal functions of Rlim in male reproduction specifically in round spermatids during spermiogenesis.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract as a conclusion from the genetic targeting experiments shown in Figure 7.

claim: Spermiogenesis represents a late stage during spermatogenesis in which post-meiotic round spermatids differentiate into mature spermatozoa.
source: Spermiogenesis represents a late stage during spermatogenesis, in which post-meiotic round spermatids differentiate into mature spermatozoa by condensation of the spermatid DNA and formation of the sperm head and tail (O'Donnell, 2014; O'Donnell et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (O'Donnell, 2014; O'Donnell et al., 2011).

claim: Spermiation involves the remodeling and reduction of cytoplasm.
source: Spermatozoa are then released into the lumen of seminiferous tubules, in a process called spermiation, which involves the remodeling and reduction of cytoplasm (França et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (França et al., 2016).

claim: The ubiquitin proteasome system plays important roles in male reproduction.
source: The ubiquitin proteasome system (UPS) plays important roles in male reproduction (Richburg et al., 2014) with a testis-specific version of the proteasome complex (Kniepert and Groettrup, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Richburg et al., 2014; Kniepert and Groettrup, 2014).

claim: The ubiquitination of proteins in cells of the testis is required for functional spermatogenesis including spermiogenesis.
source: Indeed, the ubiquitination of proteins in cells of the testis is required for functional spermatogenesis including spermiogenesis, and multiple steps during the progression of spermatogonial stem cells to mature spermatozoa critically depend on the UPS (Richburg et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Richburg et al., 2014).

claim: E3 ubiquitin ligases provide substrate specificity by selecting target proteins for ubiquitination.
source: The UPS pathway is critically dependent upon E3 ubiquitin ligases, which provide substrate specificity by selecting target proteins for ubiquitination (Metzger et al., 2014; Pickart, 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Metzger et al., 2014; Pickart, 2001).

claim: Rlim mRNA is widely expressed in many organs and cell types.
source: While Rlim mRNA is widely expressed in many organs and cell types, RLIM protein is more selectively detected (Bach et al., 1999; Ostendorff et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Bach et al., 1999; Ostendorff et al., 2006).

claim: RLIM protein is more selectively detected than Rlim mRNA.
source: While Rlim mRNA is widely expressed in many organs and cell types, RLIM protein is more selectively detected (Bach et al., 1999; Ostendorff et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Bach et al., 1999; Ostendorff et al., 2006).

claim: RLIM shuttles between the cytoplasm and nucleus in cells.
source: In cells RLIM shuttles between the cytoplasm and nucleus.
evidence: The claim is stated as established knowledge about RLIM protein behavior.

claim: Nuclear translocation of RLIM is regulated by phosphorylation.
source: Nuclear translocation is regulated by phosphorylation, and in many cell types RLIM is primarily detected in the nucleus (Jiao et al., 2013)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Jiao et al., 2013).

claim: In many cell types RLIM is primarily detected in the nucleus.
source: Nuclear translocation is regulated by phosphorylation, and in many cell types RLIM is primarily detected in the nucleus (Jiao et al., 2013)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Jiao et al., 2013).

claim: RLIM controls levels and dynamics of various proteins and protein complexes involved in transcriptional regulation.
source: where it controls not only levels and dynamics of various proteins and protein complexes involved in transcriptional regulation (Bach et al., 1999; Ostendorff et al., 2002; Krämer et al., 2003; Güngör et al., 2007; Gontan et al., 2012; Johnsen et al., 2009; Her and Chung, 2009; Huang et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2019)
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: RLIM controls its own expression via autoubiquitination.
source: but also its own expression via autoubiquitination (Ostendorff et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Ostendorff et al., 2002).

claim: RLIM promotes the survival of milk-producing alveolar cells in mammary glands of pregnant and lactating females.
source: RLIM promotes the survival of milk-producing alveolar cells in mammary glands of pregnant and lactating females (Jiao et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Jiao et al., 2012).

claim: RLIM is crucial for imprinted X chromosome inactivation (iXCI).
source: Moreover, RLIM is crucial for imprinted X chromosome inactivation (iXCI) (Shin et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2016; Gontan et al., 2018)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Shin et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2016; Gontan et al., 2018).

claim: Deletion of a maternally inherited Rlim allele results in peri-implantation lethality specifically of females due to inhibited placental trophoblast development.
source: Indeed, due to inhibited placental trophoblast development, the deletion of a maternally inherited Rlim allele results in peri-implantation lethality specifically of females (Shin et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Shin et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2016).

claim: Males systemically lacking Rlim appear to develop normally and are born at Mendelian ratios.
source: In contrast, males systemically lacking Rlim appear to develop normally, are born at Mendelian ratios and are fertile as adults (Shin et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Shin et al., 2010).

claim: Males systemically lacking Rlim are fertile as adults.
source: In contrast, males systemically lacking Rlim appear to develop normally, are born at Mendelian ratios and are fertile as adults (Shin et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Shin et al., 2010), though the current study shows functional defects in sperm.

claim: Rlim mRNA is detected in many tissues with highest levels in testis.
source: Rlim mRNA was detected in many tissues with highest levels in testis (Figure 1A), consistent with published results (Bach et al., 1999; Ostendorff et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by Northern blot data shown in Figure 1A and citations to published literature (Bach et al., 1999; Ostendorff et al., 2000).

claim: A variant Rlim mRNA band at 2.4 kb is detected in testis.
source: However, while the Rlim-encoding mRNA in most tissues migrated around 7.5 kb, a variant band at 2.4 kb was detected in testis.
evidence: The claim is supported by Northern blot data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: In sexually mature (38 dpp) animals, most reads map to exonic regions upstream of the TGA Stop codon in the Rlim locus.
source: However, most of the reads in sexually mature (38 dpp) animals mapped in exonic regions upstream of the TGA Stop codon, encompassing the 5' non-coding region and the entire open-reading frame (ORF), while most of the 3' noncoding region was underrepresented (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 1B from published datasets (Margolin et al., 2014).

claim: A consensus alternative polyadenylation site exists 69 bp downstream of the TGA Stop codon in the Rlim cDNA sequence.
source: Indeed, consistent with the length of the observed variant Rlim mRNA, closer examination the Rlim cDNA sequence revealed a consensus alternative polyadenylation site (Proudfoot, 2011) starting 69 bp downstream of the TGA Stop codon (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 1C and citation to literature on polyadenylation (Proudfoot, 2011).

claim: In mature mouse testes a short, variant Rlim RNA is generated by alternative polyadenylation.
source: Thus, in mature mouse testes a short, variant Rlim RNA is generated by alternative polyadenylation (Tian and Manley, 2017).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the RNA-seq and sequence data and supported by citation to literature on alternative polyadenylation (Tian and Manley, 2017).

claim: Western blots on protein extracts of testis, brain, and spleen confirmed high expression of full-length RLIM protein in testis.
source: Consistent with our mRNA analyses (Figure 1), western blots on protein extracts of testis, brain, and spleen confirmed high expression of full-length RLIM protein in testis (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Strong RLIM immunoreactivity is detected in specific regions of some seminiferous tubules, representing differentiating spermatogenic cells.
source: Using immunohistochemistry (IHC) on testes sections, we detected strong immunoreactivity in specific regions of some seminiferous tubules, representing differentiating spermatogenic cells (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by IHC data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Single RLIM-positive cells are detected at the periphery of all tubules.
source: Moreover, we detected single RLIM-positive cells at the periphery of all tubules.
evidence: The claim is supported by IHC data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Little to no RLIM staining is detected in males carrying a Sox2-Cre-mediated conditional knockout of the Rlim gene (cKO/YSox2-Cre).
source: Consistent with published results (Wang et al., 2016), little to no RLIM staining was detected in males carrying a Sox2-Cre (Hayashi et al., 2002) – mediated conditional knockout of the Rlim gene (cKO/YSox2-Cre), as these animals lack RLIM in somatic tissues as well as the germline (Wang et al., 2016; Shin et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by IHC data shown in Figure 2A and citations to published literature (Wang et al., 2016; Shin et al., 2014).

claim: RLIM levels are detectable but low in all spermatogenic cells around seminiferous stage II/III, including post-meiotic step 2/3 spermatids.
source: Around seminiferous stage II / III, RLIM levels are detectable but low in all spermatogenic cells, including post-meiotic step 2/3 spermatids (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by IHC co-staining data with RLIM and PNA shown in Figure 2B.

claim: RLIM levels are high in step 6–8 round spermatids (stages VI–VIII).
source: However, indicated by RLIM/PNA co-staining, RLIM levels are high in step 6–8 round spermatids (stages VI–VIII), a mid-timepoint in spermiogenesis before spermatids begin to elongate (O'Donnell, 2014; Qian et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by IHC co-staining data shown in Figure 2B and citations to literature (O'Donnell, 2014; Qian et al., 2014).

claim: RLIM protein levels are downregulated in elongating spermatids at step 10 prior to their release.
source: Thus, RLIM protein levels are low in step 1–5 spermatids, dramatically upregulated in step 6–8 spermatids, and then downregulated in elongating spermatids at step 10 prior to their release (O'Donnell et al., 2011; Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by IHC co-staining data shown in Figure 2B and citation to literature (O'Donnell et al., 2011).

claim: RLIM-positive cells located at the periphery of seminiferous tubules are Sertoli cells.
source: To identify this RLIM-positive cell type (Figure 2A), we performed IHC, co-staining with antibodies against RLIM and the Sertoli cell marker GATA1 (Yomogida et al., 1994). Positive co-staining identified these cells as Sertoli cells (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by IHC co-staining data shown in Figure 2C and citation to literature on GATA1 as a Sertoli cell marker (Yomogida et al., 1994).

claim: In cKO/YSox2-Cre and KO/Y mice the size and weight of the testis is significantly decreased when compared to fl/Y littermates.
source: Indeed, in cKO/YSox2-Cre and KO/Y mice the size and weight of the testis was significantly decreased when compared to their respective fl/Y littermates, (Figure 3A,B; Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by testis weight measurements shown in Figure 3A,B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Lower numbers of mature sperm are isolated in Caudal swim-out experiments from cKO/YSox2-Cre and KO/Y mice compared to fl/Y littermates.
source: This was accompanied by lower numbers of mature sperm isolated in Caudal swim-out experiments (Figure 3C; Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by sperm count data shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: No obvious abnormalities of specific testicular cell types during spermiogenesis are detected in animals lacking Rlim.
source: To examine plausible causes for these phenotypes, we analyzed PAS-stained testis sections. However, we did not detect obvious abnormalities of specific testicular cell types during spermiogenesis in animals lacking Rlim, and sperm release into tubules appeared normal (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D, not shown).
evidence: The claim is supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: There are no signs of increased apoptosis in the spermatogenic cells lacking Rlim.
source: Moreover, in IHC staining testes sections with antibodies against cleaved caspase 3, there were no signs of increased apoptosis in the spermatogenic cells lacking Rlim (not shown).
evidence: The claim is based on IHC staining for cleaved caspase 3, though the data is not shown.

claim: No significant differences in epididymal weight are detected between fl/Y and cKO/YSox2-Cre animals.
source: Examining epididymal epithelia, which also express RLIM (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A), revealed no significant differences in weight between fl/Y and cKO/YSox2-Cre animals (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by epididymal weight measurements shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claim: RNA-seq experiments revealed 118 down-regulated and 83 up-regulated genes in cKO/YSox2-Cre animals compared to fl/Y littermates.
source: Consistent with findings that attribute both positive and negative functions of RLIM for gene transcription (Bach et al., 1999; Gontan et al., 2012), statistical analyses revealed 118 down-regulated and 83 up-regulated genes (threshold p<0.05) in cKO/YSox2-Cre animals (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3C,D and citations to literature (Bach et al., 1999; Gontan et al., 2012).

claim: Around half of all differentially expressed genes in cKO/YSox2-Cre testes are involved in signaling (27.5%) and regulation of metabolism (22.5%).
source: Gene ontology analyses revealed that functions of these genes fell mostly in eight categories with around half of all differentially expressed genes involved in signaling (27.5%) and regulation of metabolism (22.5%), in particular regulatory functions on lipid metabolism (Figure 3E).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene ontology analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: cKO/YSox2-Cre sperm display elevated rates of morphological abnormalities, including coiled midpieces and head malformations.
source: Indeed, cKO/YSox2-Cre sperm displayed elevated rates of morphological abnormalities, including coiled midpieces and head malformations (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by sperm morphology analysis shown in Figure 4A,B.

claim: The sperm capacitation-induced phosphorylation pathways in Rlim KO sperm are similar to controls.
source: However, the sperm capacitation-induced phosphorylation pathways, acrosomal status and induced acrosome reaction in Rlim KO sperm were similar to controls as judged by western blot and PNA staining, respectively (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–E)
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot and PNA staining data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–E.

claim: cKO/YSox2-Cre sperm display decreased total motility.
source: Indeed, cKO/YSox2-Cre sperm displayed decreased total motility, and out of the total motile sperm the percentages of sperm with progressive motility was lower, while the percentages of slow and weakly motile sperm populations were higher (Figure 4C–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by CASA analysis data shown in Figure 4C–E.

claim: Out of the total motile cKO/YSox2-Cre sperm, the percentages of sperm with progressive motility is lower.
source: Indeed, cKO/YSox2-Cre sperm displayed decreased total motility, and out of the total motile sperm the percentages of sperm with progressive motility was lower, while the percentages of slow and weakly motile sperm populations were higher (Figure 4C–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by CASA analysis data shown in Figure 4C–E.

claim: The percentages of slow and weakly motile sperm populations are higher in cKO/YSox2-Cre sperm.
source: Indeed, cKO/YSox2-Cre sperm displayed decreased total motility, and out of the total motile sperm the percentages of sperm with progressive motility was lower, while the percentages of slow and weakly motile sperm populations were higher (Figure 4C–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by CASA analysis data shown in Figure 4C–E.

claim: Sperm isolated from cKO/YSox2-Cre animals yielded significantly fewer embryos reaching cleavage stage compared to fl/Y littermate controls.
source: Indeed, sperm isolated from fl/Y control animals yielded in 84.3% cleavage stage and 77% blastocyst stage embryos, compared to 67.0% and 46.8% for cKO/YSox2-Cre sperm, respectively (Figure 4F,G).
evidence: The claim is supported by IVF data shown in Figure 4F,G.

claim: Sperm isolated from cKO/YSox2-Cre animals yielded significantly fewer embryos reaching blastocyst stage compared to fl/Y littermate controls.
source: Indeed, sperm isolated from fl/Y control animals yielded in 84.3% cleavage stage and 77% blastocyst stage embryos, compared to 67.0% and 46.8% for cKO/YSox2-Cre sperm, respectively (Figure 4F,G).
evidence: The claim is supported by IVF data shown in Figure 4F,G.

claim: The rate of blastocysts per cleavage staged embryos is 92% for fl/Y sperm and only 70% for cKO/YSox2-Cre sperm.
source: Moreover, the rate of blastocysts per cleavage staged embryos was 92% of for fl/Y sperm and only 70% for cKO/YSox2-Cre (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F)
evidence: The claim is supported by IVF data analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Lack of Rlim negatively affects embryonic development under in vitro conditions.
source: suggesting that lack of Rlim negatively affects embryonic development under in vitro conditions.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the IVF data showing reduced developmental rates.

claim: Significantly more Rlim cKO/YSox2-Cre sperm display cytoplasmic droplets in the midpiece compared to fl/Y sperm.
source: Interrogating sperm via scanning EM (SEM) revealed significantly more Rlim cKO/YSox2-Cre sperm displaying cytoplasmic droplets in the midpiece, and these droplets were also increased in size as measured using ImageJ software (Figure 5B–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by SEM data shown in Figure 5B–D.

claim: Cytoplasmic droplets in cKO/YSox2-Cre sperm are increased in size compared to fl/Y sperm.
source: Interrogating sperm via scanning EM (SEM) revealed significantly more Rlim cKO/YSox2-Cre sperm displaying cytoplasmic droplets in the midpiece, and these droplets were also increased in size as measured using ImageJ software (Figure 5B–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by SEM data and quantification shown in Figure 5B–D.

claim: The sizes of cytoplasmic droplets in testicular sperm are significantly increased in cKO/YSox2-Cre compared to fl/Y.
source: Again, the sizes of cytoplasmic droplets in testicular sperm were significantly increased (Figure 6C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by SEM data and quantification shown in Figure 6C,D.

claim: The midpieces from cKO sperm are highly vulnerable to rupturing.
source: We noted that the midpieces from cKO sperm were highly vulnerable to rupturing, while the prevalence of coiled midpieces appeared similar between cKO and control sperm (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by morphological analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: A low number of sperm exhibit duplicated axonemes specifically in Rlim cKO/YSox2-Cre but not in fl/Y sperm.
source: Moreover, we detected a low number of sperm that exhibited duplicated axonemes specifically in Rlim cKO/YSox2-Cre but not in fl/Y sperm (Figure 6B; Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by SEM and TEM data shown in Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: TEM on testes sections confirmed the occurrence of duplicated axonemes in cKO/YSox2-Cre sperm.
source: Transmission EM (TEM) on testes sections confirmed the occurrence of duplicated axonemes in cKO/YSox2-Cre sperm as well as head malformations, while the overall structural integrity of the sperm tail appeared normal (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–D)
evidence: The claim is supported by TEM data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–D.

claim: The overall structural integrity of the sperm tail appears normal in cKO/YSox2-Cre sperm.
source: Transmission EM (TEM) on testes sections confirmed the occurrence of duplicated axonemes in cKO/YSox2-Cre sperm as well as head malformations, while the overall structural integrity of the sperm tail appeared normal (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–D)
evidence: The claim is supported by TEM data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–D.

claim: No signs of decreased chromatin packaging in sperm heads are detected in cKO/YSox2-Cre sperm.
source: and no signs of decreased chromatin packaging in sperm heads was detected as judged by sperm head density.
evidence: The claim is based on TEM observations of sperm head density.

claim: The cytoplasmic pockets in the Rlim cKO sperm heads appear more pronounced in sperm of the epididymal Caput region.
source: Interestingly, the cytoplasmic pockets in the Rlim cKO sperm heads appeared more pronounced in sperm of the epididymal Caput region (Figure 6E,F).
evidence: The claim is supported by TEM data shown in Figure 6E,F.

claim: Similar numbers of Sertoli cells are present in testes with or without Rlim.
source: Counting GATA4-positive cells within seminiferous tubules, IHC revealed similar numbers of Sertoli cells in testes with or without Rlim (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A,B)
evidence: The claim is supported by IHC data and quantification shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Rlim is not required for Sertoli cell development and differentiation.
source: indicating that Rlim is not required for Sertoli cell development and differentiation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that Sertoli cell numbers are similar in testes with or without Rlim.

claim: No major structural deficiencies are detected in Sertoli cells lacking Rlim including the formation of apical ectoplasmic specialization (ES) or the apical tubulobulbar complex (TBC).
source: Moreover, analyzing specific Sertoli cell structures involved in spermiation in testis sections via TEM, we did not detect major structural deficiencies in cells lacking Rlim including the formation of apical ectoplasmic specialization (ES) or the apical tubulobulbar complex (TBC), and no obvious signs of defective cytoplasmic reduction (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by TEM data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: Rlim cKO/YNgn3-Cre mice display decreased testis weights compared to littermate controls.
source: Indeed, Rlim cKO/YNgn3-Cre mice displayed decreased testis weights and numbers of mature sperm isolated in caudal swim-out experiments (Figure 7B,C, respectively).
evidence: The claim is supported by testis weight measurements shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Rlim cKO/YNgn3-Cre mice display decreased numbers of mature sperm isolated in caudal swim-out experiments compared to littermate controls.
source: Indeed, Rlim cKO/YNgn3-Cre mice displayed decreased testis weights and numbers of mature sperm isolated in caudal swim-out experiments (Figure 7B,C, respectively).
evidence: The claim is supported by sperm count data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: No significant effects on testes weights and sperm numbers are measured in cKO/YSf1-Cre animals compared to littermate controls.
source: In contrast, no significant effects on testes weights and sperm numbers were measured in cKO/YSf1-Cre animals.
evidence: The claim is supported by testis weight and sperm count data shown in Figure 7B,C.

claim: SEM analyses revealed significantly increased numbers of sperm containing cytoplasmic droplets in cKO/YNgn3-Cre animals compared with cKO/YSf1-Cre animals and their respective littermate controls.
source: Consistent with these findings, SEM analyses of Caudal swim-out sperm revealed significantly increased numbers of sperm containing cytoplasmic droplets in cKO/YNgn3-Cre animals when compared with cKO/YSf1-Cre animals and their respective littermate controls (Figure 7D).
evidence: The claim is supported by SEM data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: The droplet sizes in cKO/YNgn3-Cre sperm are increased compared to controls.
source: Moreover, focusing on sperm with cytoplasmic droplets, the droplet sizes in cKO/YNgn3-Cre sperm were increased (Figure 7E,F), similar to those of cKO/YSox2-Cre sperm (Figure 5C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by SEM data and quantification shown in Figure 7E,F.

claim: IVF experiments using cKO/YNgn3-Cre sperm yielded 62% cleavage stage and 33% blastocyst stage embryos compared to 76% and 58% for control sperm.
source: IVF experiments using swim-out sperm yielded in 76% cleavage stage and 58% blastocyst stage embryos for control, compared to 62% and 33% for cKO/YNgn3-Cre sperm, respectively (Figure 7G)
evidence: The claim is supported by IVF data shown in Figure 7G.

claim: The phenotypes in males systemically lacking Rlim are largely recapitulated by cKO/YNgn3-Cre but not cKO/YSf1-Cre mice.
source: Thus, the phenotypes in males systemically lacking Rlim are largely recapitulated by cKO/YNgn3-Cre but not cKO/YSf1-Cre mice, demonstrating functions of Rlim in the spermatogenic cell lineage.
evidence: The claim is inferred from comparing the phenotypes of different Cre-mediated deletions shown in Figure 7.

claim: The upregulated expression of Rlim in round spermatids plays important functions for the reduction of cytoplasmic volume in sperm.
source: Our combined results provide strong evidence that the upregulated expression of Rlim in round spermatids plays important functions for the reduction of cytoplasmic volume in sperm.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the combined genetic and phenotypic data presented in the study.

claim: The appearance of a variant Rlim mRNA in males coincides with sexual maturation.
source: The appearance of a variant mRNA in males coincides with sexual maturation, suggesting that this form is predominantly expressed in differentiating round spermatids, which express high levels of RLIM protein (Figure 2A)
evidence: The claim is inferred from the RNA-seq data showing the variant mRNA appears at 38 dpp (sexually mature) and the IHC data showing high RLIM protein in round spermatids.

claim: Alternative mRNAs display different time of synthesis, mRNA stability and/or translational efficiency.
source: Indeed, alternative mRNAs display different time of synthesis, mRNA stability and/or translational efficiency (Tian and Manley, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Tian and Manley, 2017).

claim: Rlim joins many X-linked genes that are reactivated after meiotic sex chromosome inactivation (MSCI).
source: Thus, Rlim joins many X-linked genes that are reactivated after meiotic sex chromosome inactivation (MSCI) (Ernst et al., 2019)
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that RLIM protein is upregulated post-meiotically and supported by citation to literature on MSCI (Ernst et al., 2019).

claim: The downregulation of RLIM in elongating spermatocytes coincides with a change in transcriptional and chromatin dynamics at this stage.
source: Moreover, the downregulation of RLIM in elongating spermatocytes coincides with a change in transcriptional and chromatin dynamics at this stage (Ernst et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observed RLIM downregulation pattern and supported by citation to literature (Ernst et al., 2019).

claim: RLIM is detected in most/all round spermatids, including those that presumably harbor a Y chromosome.
source: Even though Rlim is X-linked, the finding that the RLIM protein is detected in most/all round spermatids, including those that presumably harbor a Y chromosome, is explained by the fact that cytoplasmic bridges exist between spermatids and that RLIM efficiently shuttles between nuclei in heterokaryon cells (Jiao et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is based on IHC observations and explained by known biology of cytoplasmic bridges and RLIM shuttling, supported by citation (Jiao et al., 2013).

claim: Many genes are affected in testes lacking Rlim influencing various cellular functions including signaling and metabolism.
source: Our RNA-seq analyses indicate that many genes are affected in testes lacking Rlim influencing various cellular functions including signaling and metabolism (Figure 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Many of the differentially expressed genes might be affected indirectly by Rlim deletion.
source: As Rlim regulates transcriptional factors (Bach et al., 1999; Ostendorff et al., 2002; Krämer et al., 2003; Güngör et al., 2007; Gontan et al., 2012; Johnsen et al., 2009; Her and Chung, 2009; Huang et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2019), it is thus likely that many of the differentially expressed genes (Figure 3D,E) might be affected indirectly.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the known function of RLIM as a regulator of transcription factors, supported by multiple citations.

claim: Excess cytoplasm affects sperm motility, morphology including head morphology as well as fertilization potential.
source: Because excess cytoplasm affects sperm motility, morphology including head morphology as well as fertilization potential (Cooper, 2011; Rengan et al., 2012)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Cooper, 2011; Rengan et al., 2012).

claim: The increased cytoplasmic volume is likely responsible for much of the defects detected in sperm lacking Rlim.
source: it is likely that the increased cytoplasmic volume is responsible for much of the defects detected in sperm lacking Rlim.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observed phenotypes and known effects of excess cytoplasm on sperm function.

claim: The midpiece cytoplasm is particularly important for sperm osmoregulation.
source: Moreover, as the midpiece cytoplasm is particularly important for sperm osmoregulation (Cooper, 2011; Rengan et al., 2012)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Cooper, 2011; Rengan et al., 2012).

claim: An increased size of cytoplasmic droplets is predicted to render sperm more vulnerable to osmotic challenges.
source: an increased size of cytoplasmic droplets is predicted to render sperm more vulnerable to osmotic challenges, which may ultimately lead to midpiece rupturing (Figure 6).
evidence: The claim is inferred from known biology of cytoplasmic droplets and osmoregulation, and supported by the observation of midpiece rupturing in Figure 6.

claim: Increased sperm cytoplasm has been associated with higher activities of specific enzymes of the energy pathway including G6PDH.
source: In this context, an increased sperm cytoplasm has been associated with higher activities of specific enzymes of the energy pathway including G6PDH (Aitken et al., 1994; Yuan et al., 2013)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Aitken et al., 1994; Yuan et al., 2013).

claim: G6PDH diverts glucose metabolism away from glycolysis toward the pentose pathway.
source: which diverts glucose metabolism away from glycolysis toward the pentose pathway.
evidence: The claim is stated as established knowledge about G6PDH function.

claim: Increased G6PDH activity might be partially responsible for the decreased Acetyl-CoA levels measured in sperm lacking Rlim.
source: It is thus tempting to speculate that increased G6PDH activity might be partially responsible for the decreased Acetyl-CoA levels measured in sperm lacking Rlim (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is speculative, connecting the metabolomic data in Figure 5A with known effects of G6PDH.

claim: Inefficient cytoplasmic reduction during spermiogenesis/spermiation renders Rlim KO sperm vulnerable to adequately adjust to the changing environment during transit through the epididymis.
source: Our combined data suggests that inefficient cytoplasmic reduction during spermiogenesis/spermiation renders Rlim KO sperm vulnerable to adequately adjust to the changing environment that occurs during transit through the epididymis (Gervasi and Visconti, 2017; Sullivan and Saez, 2013) leading to functional defects.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined data and supported by citations about the epididymal environment (Gervasi and Visconti, 2017; Sullivan and Saez, 2013).

claim: Lack of RLIM specifically in round spermatids is responsible for much of the observed sperm phenotype.
source: Our combined data reveals that lack of RLIM specifically in round spermatids is responsible for much of the observed sperm phenotype.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the genetic targeting experiments comparing Ngn3-Cre and Sf1-Cre mediated deletions.

claim: Rlim in Sertoli cells is not involved in the regulation of spermiogenesis.
source: In contrast, targeting the Rlim cKO via Sf1-Cre to Sertoli cells failed to induce a testis/sperm phenotype and providing strong evidence that Rlim in Sertoli cells is not involved in the regulation of spermiogenesis provided by this cell type.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the lack of phenotype in Sf1-Cre mediated deletion shown in Figure 7.

claim: Rlim adds to a very limited number of genes in the spermatogenic cell lineage that regulate the cytoplasmic reduction/droplet size.
source: Therefore, Rlim adds to a very limited number of genes in the spermatogenic cell lineage that regulate the cytoplasmic reduction/droplet size (Zheng et al., 2007; Mikolcevic et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Zheng et al., 2007; Mikolcevic et al., 2012) identifying other genes with similar functions.

claim: A deleterious mutation in the Rlim gene would shift selective evolutionary pressure entirely on females leading to a gender bias toward males in a mouse population over time.
source: Considering early lethality of female mouse embryos with a maternally transmitted Rlim mutation (Shin et al., 2010), mathematical modeling of this exclusively female phenotype indicates that a deleterious mutation in the Rlim gene would shift selective evolutionary pressure entirely on females leading to a gender bias toward males in a mouse population over time (Jiao et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Shin et al., 2010; Jiao et al., 2012) on the female-specific lethality and mathematical modeling.

claim: Gender biases in mouse populations represent an unfavorable strategy for reproduction.
source: Because gender biases in mouse populations represent an unfavorable strategy for reproduction (Hamilton, 1967)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Hamilton, 1967).

claim: The observed functions of Rlim during male reproduction will contribute to counter-act gender biases induced by its female function.
source: it is likely that the observed functions of Rlim during male reproduction will contribute to counter-act gender biases induced by its female function.
evidence: The claim is speculative, inferring an evolutionary role for Rlim's male function based on the female-specific lethality.

claim: In addition to crucial epigenetic functions in female embryogenesis and reproduction, the E3 ubiquitin ligase RLIM also occupies important roles during the reproduction of male mice.
source: In summary, our data provide first evidence that in addition to crucial epigenetic functions in female embryogenesis and reproduction, the E3 ubiquitin ligase RLIM also occupies important roles during the reproduction of male mice.
evidence: The claim is a summary conclusion of the study's findings.

claim: Sertoli cells are known to regulate cytoplasmic reduction in spermatozoa.
source: Even though Sertoli cells are known to regulate cytoplasmic reduction in spermatozoa (O'Donnell, 2014; O'Donnell et al., 2011)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (O'Donnell, 2014; O'Donnell et al., 2011).

claim: Cytoplasmic reduction during spermiogenesis is regulated by Rlim expressed in the spermatogenic cell lineage.
source: our genetic analyses reveal that this activity is mediated by Rlim expressed in the spermatogenic cell lineage.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the genetic targeting experiments shown in Figure 7.
